extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, researchers studying peer review, and policy‑makers in biomedical publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review of evidence about editorial peer review processes and their effects on the quality of reports of biomedical research; presents categories of editorial processes, outcome domains for measuring quality, and measurement guidance (ideal vs surrogate indicators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of editorial peer review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The processes applied to paper or electronic articles can be divided into procedures aimed at assessing and ensuring scientific quality (editorial peer review), technical processes (e.g. copy‑editing), and administrative processes (e.g. tracking submissions). This review assesses the effects of processes undertaken as part of editorial peer review of original research studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial peer review processes are grouped and assessed as: different ways of screening submissions; different ways of assigning submissions (choosing/assigning assessors); different ways of masking submissions (concealing author and/or assessor identity and background); different ways of eliciting internal opinions (within the publishing organisation); different ways of eliciting external opinions (outside assessors); different (group or single person) decision‑making procedures; different types of feedback to author(s) and subsequent revision of submissions; combinations of the above; and any other process considered editorial peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study design inclusion criteria for evidence about peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of comparative studies included to evaluate peer review processes: randomised controlled trials, quasi‑randomised controlled trials, interrupted time series, before and after studies, and other observational studies where there was some attempt to control for confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluded: surveys comparing editorial practice or editorial outcomes with characteristics of journals or reviewers, and review articles. The review sought comparative designs with two or more groups generated by random or other appropriate methods, reporting original research (not reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcome: quality of the published report
rubrics_metrics.description: The main outcome sought was the quality of the published report, however measured; the measurement of quality should reflect the aims of editorial peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality should be measured at an ideal level (true outcomes) where possible, otherwise by pragmatic surrogate outcomes (ranked) or process measures. See specific outcome domains (importance, usefulness, relevance, methodological soundness, ethics, completeness, accuracy) for concrete definitions and indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study findings have a potential high impact on health and healthcare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: Changes in health status or changes in healthcare delivery. Surrogate rank 1: citation rates, media coverage. Surrogate rank 2: tone and content of assessors' and editors' reports, correspondence. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures (e.g. speed or cost of reviewing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study contributes significantly to the scientific debate or knowledge on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: Contributes significantly within a systematic review of the topic; narrows confidence intervals around estimates of effect. Surrogate rank 1: contributes significantly within a review of the topic. Surrogate rank 2: assessors' and editors' reports, correspondence. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures (e.g. speed or cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study topic is relevant to the journal, its aims and to the readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: Is relevant and consistent with the aims and readership of the journal confirmed by survey. Surrogate rank 1: citation rates. Surrogate rank 2: editors' and assessors' reports, correspondence, Internet hit rates. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological soundness (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods used can answer the study question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: Study findings are replicated several times across settings where studies appear to have been well‑conducted. Surrogate rank 1: closeness of fit between methods and an 'evidence‑based' methodological checklist. Surrogate rank 2: editors' and assessors' reports. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures (e.g. speed or cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical conduct and reporting (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The study has been carried out and reported honestly; its limitations are explicit and unnecessary harm to humans or animals has been avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: No divergence between reality and the report; rights of humans and animals safeguarded; privacy and informed consent maintained. Surrogate rank 1: no duplicate publication, no complaints from participants, ethical clearance granted. Surrogate rank 2: editors' and assessors' reports, correspondence, reputational indicators (highly reputable institution/investigators). Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of reporting (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: All relevant information is presented; there is no selective presentation of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: Raw data match aggregate data and the text is complete. Surrogate rank 1: the text is complete. Surrogate rank 2: correspondence. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of reporting (outcome domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: All relevant information is a true reflection of what went on; measurements truly reflect magnitude of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicator: measurements accurately reflect magnitude; figures add up. Surrogate rank 1: figures add up and correspondence supports accuracy. Surrogate rank 2: correspondence. Surrogate rank 3: process‑centred measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold‑standard editorial process (combined outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gold standard editorial process is one that produces studies that are important, appropriate to the publication medium, useful, original, methodologically sound, ethical, complete and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the outcome domains above to operationalise 'gold standard'. Measurements should prioritise ideal indicators where possible; moving rightwards to surrogates and process measures reduces the indicator's strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of outcome indicators (ideal → surrogate → process)
rubrics_metrics.description: As one moves from ideal indicators to surrogates to process indicators, the importance of the chosen indicator decreases and its surrogate nature increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal (true outcomes) are highest quality measures; surrogate indicators are ranked (rank 1 better than rank 2, etc.); process‑centred measures (speed, cost) are third‑rank and least direct measures of study quality. Prefer higher‑rank indicators when synthesising evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masking/blinding of authors and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Different ways of masking submissions (concealing the identity and background of the authors and/or the assessors) and of revealing reviewer identity (open/signed vs anonymous) are key process variables thought to affect bias and review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured outcomes include effects on review quality scores, ability to detect deliberate errors, tone/politeness of reviews, time taken, and willingness of reviewers to participate. Evidence is mixed: some trials showed blinding produced different review quality; others found no effect. Open/signed review may increase courtesy and time spent and reduce likelihood of rejection but can reduce reviewer participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of checklists and standardisation media
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of checklists (e.g. submission checklists, statistical/referee checklists) to standardise evaluation of submissions is an intervention to improve editorial outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: BMJ 36‑item checklist for economic submissions; 12–24 item statistical checklists. Evidence suggests checklists can help editors manage submissions and improve statistical quality of published studies; their effect on overall submission quality may be limited. Checklists serve as surrogate/standardisation media and may be assessed by pre/post comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training, feedback and manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions include voluntary workshops, formal interactive training, short training packages, written feedback to reviewers, and training manuals and structured checklists for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence shows small, short‑term or non‑sustained improvements from some training packages (e.g. self‑study CD improved error detection transiently), but overall many trials found no improvement in subsequent review performance from brief workshops or simple written feedback. Longer, more intensive interventions require further evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication media and reviewer contact procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of communicating with reviewers and means of eliciting reviews (e.g. advance phone warning, ask‑first fax, posting manuscripts for open Internet comment) are process variables evaluated for effects on turnaround, response rates, and review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'askfirst' vs 'justsend' affects initial declines and need for substitute reviewers but may not change review quality; open Internet comment yields few external comments and little change in commissioned review quality. Cost and speed trade‑offs are important process metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dedicated methodology/statistical reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning dedicated methodological and statistical reviewers to manuscripts to improve methodological/statistical quality of published reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies compare comments to authors from methodology/statistical reviewers versus regular reviewers and assess whether this improves the detection of methodological/statistical problems and the quality of published articles. Evidence mixed; this is a specific process to evaluate in trials or content analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality assessment instrument items (RQI / Black instrument / others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific item lists used to assess the quality of peer reviews include items such as importance of research question, originality, methods, presentation/organisation, constructiveness of comments, substantiation of comments, interpretation of results, writing style and politeness/courteousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from trials: van Rooyen RQI items (importance of research question, originality, method, presentation, constructiveness of comments, substantiation of comments, interpretation of results, politeness of tone), Black instrument items (importance of research question, originality, methods, organisation, writing style and tone), and other 4–7 item scales including courteousness and provision of evidence to support views. These instruments are used as surrogate measures of review quality and vary across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measurement level: ideal versus pragmatic (true outcomes vs surrogates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement should be made at an ideal level (true outcomes used as indicators of quality) when possible, otherwise by pragmatic surrogate outcomes or process measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal indicators (e.g. changes in health outcomes) are preferred but often infeasible; surrogate indicators (citations, editor/assessor judgments) and process measures (speed, cost) are commonly used. When synthesising evidence, consider indicator rank and generalisability; third‑rank (process) indicators are least direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of data and reports to be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports evaluated should be original research submitted to biomedical journals (not reviews or commentaries); reports may be published or unpublished, and peer reviewers themselves are sometimes subjects of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence syntheses should exclude review articles and focus on original research submissions. The unit of analysis and the level of masking or intervention (manuscript, reviewer, editor) must be specified in study designs.
